title: Commodore 64 for Beginners: BASIC, Sprites, Sound, Assembly and C
subtitle: Program a real Commodore 64 inside the app: start with BASIC, then the screen, sprites, sound, joystick, the ports and a small game, then gentle machine code and C with cc65
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A true beginners course on the Commodore 64 in 18 chapters. You start at the READY prompt with BASIC V2 (programs, variables, loops, subroutines, PEEK and POKE), then drive the hardware: the screen, sprites, SID sound, joystick and keyboard, and the ports (control ports, user port, serial, cassette, expansion), and build a small game. Then you meet 6510 machine code (registers, loops, the KERNAL, raster timing and interrupts) and C with the cc65 compiler, and finish with tape and disk. Every chapter has numbered figures and tables, a recap, a memory trick, an expanded ELI5 and a concept map. 17 hands-on labs (64 levels) run on a cycle-exact C64 inside the app with its original BASIC; assembly is assembled in the lab and C is compiled in the lab with cc65. Credits: the emulator core is c64.wasm from hayesmaker/c64-ready (MIT licence, based on lvllvl's c64.js); it contains the original Commodore KERNAL, BASIC and character ROMs, which remain the property of their copyright holders and are not covered by the MIT licence. C labs use the cc65 toolchain (zlib licence) compiled to WebAssembly as packaged by 8bitworkshop. The course text, figures and labs are original.

chapters.title: Meet the Commodore 64

maps.title: The C64

summary: The Commodore 64 came out in 1982 and became one of the best-selling home computers ever. It switches on in about a second, straight into a programming language called BASIC, so every owner was invited to program it.

Inside are a processor, 64 kilobytes of memory, and three kinds of helper chips: one for pictures, one for sound, and two for keyboard, joysticks and ports. You control all of them with plain numbers.
In this course you program a real C64. The labs run an exact copy of the machine, with its original BASIC, right inside the app. No hardware or setup is needed.

glossary.def: Short for Commodore 64, a home computer from 1982.
The simple programming language built into the C64.
The C64's processor (CPU), a close relative of the 6502.
The video chip: text, colours and sprites.
The sound chip, with three voices.
Complex Interface Adapter: two chips for keyboard, joysticks, timers and ports.
Typing a command without a line number, so it runs at once.
A program that behaves exactly like another computer.

keyPoints: The C64 starts straight into BASIC and shows READY.
A command without a line number runs at once: that is direct mode.
PRINT shows text and the answers to sums.
POKE writes a number into a memory cell; cell 53280 is the border colour.
The chips (VIC-II, SID, CIAs) are controlled by writing numbers into their cells.

items: ELI5. Imagine a toy box with a little brain inside, plus helpers. One helper paints pictures, one sings, and two keep an eye on the buttons and the doors. The brain gives orders by writing numbers on sticky notes in special mailboxes, and each helper reads its own mailbox.

Now the real words. The brain is the 6510 processor. The painter is the VIC-II video chip, the singer is the SID sound chip, and the watchers are the two CIA chips for the keyboard, joysticks and ports. The mailboxes are memory cells. When you switch on, the C64 starts BASIC and shows READY. A command without a line number runs straight away, which is called direct mode.
Try it. In the first lab type print 6*7 and watch the answer appear. Then type poke 53280,0 and the border turns black.
If you remember one thing: you talk to every part of the C64 by putting numbers into the right memory cells.

Imagine a toy box that holds a small brain and a few helpers. The brain (the 6510 processor) does the thinking. One helper paints the picture (the VIC-II), one sings (the SID), and two watch the keyboard, the joysticks and the sockets (the CIAs). They all share one road of wires, called the bus.
(See Figure 1.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.1. The 6510 processor and its helpers share one bus. Each helper chip is a handful of memory cells.

items: The surprising part is how you give orders to the helpers. Each one appears as a few numbered memory cells. Put a number into the right cell and the chip obeys. The border colour, for example, lives in cell 53280. That is the whole trick behind most of this course. (See Table 1.1 below.)

head: Part
What it does

items: When you switch on, the C64 shows a blue screen with a banner, the amount of memory free for BASIC, and the word READY. A flashing square, the cursor, waits for you. (See Figure 1.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.2. The READY prompt. A line without a number runs at once; a numbered line is stored for later.

items: Anything you type and finish with RETURN is read by BASIC. If the line starts with a number, it is stored as part of a program. If it does not, it runs straight away. That second way is called direct mode, and it turns the C64 into a calculator.

lesson.code:
print 6*7
print "hello"
poke 53280,0

items: The first line prints 42 (BASIC puts a space before positive numbers, where the minus sign would go). The second prints HELLO. The third makes the border black. A star means multiply, a slash means divide.

Typing on the C64 is a little different. It shows capital letters by default; in the lab you can type small letters and they appear as capitals. Shifted keys give graphics symbols. RETURN finishes a line. RUN/STOP stops a running program.
If things get stuck, the lab has a Reset button, which is like switching off and on.

A word about mistakes: you cannot break the C64 by typing. The worst that happens is a message such as ?SYNTAX ERROR, which means BASIC did not understand the line. Read it, fix the typo, press RETURN again.

The labs run c64.wasm from the open-source project c64-ready, which copies the real machine cycle by cycle. It uses the original Commodore ROMs, so the BASIC you type is exactly what owners typed in 1982.
Memory trick: Brain, painter, singer, watchers. The 6510 Brain thinks, the VIC-II Paints, the SID Sings, the CIAs Watch the keys and ports.

chapters.title: Your first programs

maps.title: Programs
links: Programs | are made of | Numbered lines
Numbered lines | kept | In number order

summary: A program is a list of numbered lines. BASIC keeps them sorted by number and RUN starts at the lowest one. You can add, change or delete lines at any time.
You will learn PRINT, RUN, LIST, NEW, GOTO, END and REM, and how to stop a program that runs forever.
By the end you can write short programs, change them, and know what each line does.

glossary.def: The number at the start of a program line, from 0 to 63999.
Starts the program at its lowest line.
Shows the program lines.
Erases the program in memory.
Jumps to another line.
A remark: a note for people that BASIC ignores.
The key that stops a running program (BREAK).

keyPoints: A numbered line is stored; RUN starts at the lowest number.
Lines are kept sorted by number, whatever order you type them.
Typing a number on its own deletes that line; retyping a line replaces it.
GOTO jumps; a GOTO back up makes a loop that runs until RUN/STOP.
REM lines are notes for people; END stops the program.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Meet the Commodore 64:
• The C64 starts straight into BASIC and shows READY.
• A command without a line number runs at once: that is direct mode.
• PRINT shows text and the answers to sums.
• POKE writes a number into a memory cell; cell 53280 is the border colour.
• The chips (VIC-II, SID, CIAs) are controlled by writing numbers into their cells.

ELI5. Imagine giving a friend a stack of numbered cards with instructions. They always do the cards in number order, card 10, then 20, then 30, even if you handed them over shuffled. You can swap a card by writing a new one with the same number.

Now the real words. A program is a list of numbered lines. BASIC keeps them sorted, RUN starts at the lowest, LIST shows them and NEW erases them. GOTO jumps to another line; jumping back up makes a loop that runs until you press RUN/STOP. REM lines are notes that BASIC skips.
Try it. Write three print lines numbered 10, 20 and 30, then type them in a different order and see that RUN still follows the numbers.
If you remember one thing: the line number decides the order, so leave gaps of ten to slip new lines in.
Type a line that starts with a number and nothing seems to happen. BASIC quietly stores it. Type RUN and the stored lines run in number order. Type LIST to see them again.

lesson.code:
10 print "ready"
20 print "set"
30 print "go"
run

items: The number decides the order, not the typing order. If you type line 30 first and line 10 last, BASIC still runs 10, 20, 30. That is why programmers count in tens: you can slip a line 15 in later without retyping anything. (See Figure 2.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.1. Lines are sorted by number. RUN starts at the lowest; GOTO jumps anywhere.

items: Editing is just as simple. Type a line with an existing number to replace it. Type the number alone and press RETURN to delete the line. NEW erases the whole program, so use it with care. (See Table 2.1 below.)

What it does

items: GOTO sends BASIC to another line. Jump back up and you have made a loop that never ends:

lesson.code:
10 print "c64 rules! ";
20 goto 10

items: The semicolon at the end of line 10 tells PRINT not to start a new line, so the words fill the screen. Press RUN/STOP to break in. BASIC answers BREAK IN 10 and READY, and your program is still there.
PRINT has a few more tricks. A comma moves to the next column of ten characters. Several items can follow PRINT, separated by semicolons. Text goes in quotes; sums do not.
REM lines are notes. BASIC skips them, but they help you remember why a line is there. END stops the program, which matters later when you put helper lines after the main part.
Memory trick: Number means later. A line with a Number is kept for Later; no number means Now.

chapters.title: Variables and INPUT

maps.title: Variables
links: Variables | have a quirk | Two-letter names
INPUT | wrong kind gives | REDO FROM START
A | text in it gives | TYPE MISMATCH

summary: A variable is a named box that holds a value. BASIC V2 has three kinds: decimal numbers, whole numbers (ending in %) and text (ending in $).
INPUT asks the user for a value and puts it in a variable, so programs can react to people.
You will also meet BASIC V2's oddest rule: only the first two letters of a name count.

glossary.def: A named box that holds a value.
A piece of text; its variable name ends in $.
A whole-number variable; its name ends in %.
Waits for the user to type a value and RETURN.
The error for putting text in a number box or the other way round.
A sum or a join that BASIC works out, such as A*2 or N$+"!".

keyPoints: A=7 makes a number box; N$="ADA" makes a text box; A%=7 makes a whole-number box.
Text in a number box gives ?TYPE MISMATCH ERROR.
Only the first two letters of a name count: SCORE and SCALE are the same variable.
INPUT "question";A waits for an answer and stores it.
PRINT joins items with semicolons; + joins strings.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Your first programs:
• A numbered line is stored; RUN starts at the lowest number.
• Lines are kept sorted by number, whatever order you type them.
• Typing a number on its own deletes that line; retyping a line replaces it.
• GOTO jumps; a GOTO back up makes a loop that runs until RUN/STOP.
• REM lines are notes for people; END stops the program.
ELI5. Imagine a shelf of labelled boxes. Some boxes only take numbers, some only take whole numbers, and some only take words. If you try to put a word in a number box, the shelf complains.

Now the real words. Variables are named boxes. A plain name like A holds any number, A% holds whole numbers, and A$ holds text. Putting text in a number box gives ?TYPE MISMATCH ERROR. INPUT asks the person at the keyboard for a value. In BASIC V2 only the first two letters of a name count, so SCORE and SCALE are the same box.
Try it. Write 10 input "name";n$ and 20 print "hi ";n$, run it, and type your name.
If you remember one thing: the last character of the name tells you what kind of box it is: $ for words, % for whole numbers.
Think of labelled boxes on a shelf. A=7 puts 7 into a box labelled A. PRINT A shows what is inside. A=A+1 takes the 7 out, adds one and puts 8 back. (See Figure 3.1 below.) (See Table 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.1. The three kinds of variable: decimal numbers, whole numbers and text.

lesson.code:
10 a=7
20 b=6
30 print a*b
40 n$="ada"
50 print "hello, ";n$

items: Names start with a letter and may contain letters and digits, but BASIC V2 only looks at the first two characters. SCORE and SCALE are both the box SC. Names also may not contain a keyword: a name like TOTAL hides the word TO and gives ?SYNTAX ERROR. Short names such as S, SC and HI are safest.
INPUT lets the person at the keyboard fill a box. It prints the question, a question mark, and waits. When they press RETURN, the answer goes in the variable.

lesson.code:
10 input "how old are you";a
20 print "next year you are";a+1
30 input "name";n$
40 print "hi ";n$;"!"

items: If someone types letters where a number was expected, BASIC answers ?REDO FROM START and asks again. Strings can be joined with a plus sign: N$+"!" makes a new, longer string. Strings cannot be multiplied, and numbers cannot be joined to strings with plus; use PRINT with semicolons instead.
A few useful helpers turn one kind into another. STR$(5) is the text "5". VAL("12") is the number 12. LEN(N$) counts the characters. LEFT$, RIGHT$ and MID$ cut pieces out of a string.
Memory trick: Dollar for words, percent for wholes. A $ box holds words (strings), a % box holds whole numbers, a plain name holds any number.

chapters.title: Decisions and loops

maps.title: Control
links: Control | repeats with | FOR and NEXT
Control | decides with | IF and THEN
FOR and NEXT | counts by | STEP
IF and THEN | tests with | Comparisons
IF and THEN | false skips | Rest of the line
Comparisons | combined by | AND OR NOT

summary: Programs become useful when they can repeat and decide. FOR and NEXT repeat a block a set number of times. IF and THEN do something only when a test is true.
You will count up and down with STEP, build times tables, and branch on the user's answer.
These two ideas, repeat and decide, are behind every game and tool you will write.

glossary.def: A loop with a counter that runs a set number of times.
How much the counter changes each time round.
Runs the rest of the line only when the test is true.
A test such as A>10 that is true or false.
Combine or flip conditions.
A loop inside another loop.

keyPoints: FOR I=1 TO 10 ... NEXT I repeats with I counting 1 to 10.
STEP -1 counts down; STEP 2 counts in twos.
IF test THEN action runs the action only when the test is true.
Tests use = <> < > <= >=, combined with AND, OR, NOT.
When IF is false, BASIC skips the rest of that line and goes to the next line.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Variables and INPUT:
• A=7 makes a number box; N$="ADA" makes a text box; A%=7 makes a whole-number box.
• Text in a number box gives ?TYPE MISMATCH ERROR.
• Only the first two letters of a name count: SCORE and SCALE are the same variable.
• INPUT "question";A waits for an answer and stores it.
• PRINT joins items with semicolons; + joins strings.
ELI5. Imagine running laps around a track with a counter clicking each lap, and a coach at the gate who only lets you through if you show the right ticket.

Now the real words. FOR and NEXT repeat a block with a counter, and STEP decides how much it changes each lap; STEP -1 counts down. IF and THEN are the coach: the rest of the line only runs when the test is true. Tests use =, <>, <, >, <= and >=, and can be combined with AND and OR.
Try it. Count down from 10 to 1 with STEP -1 and print LIFTOFF at the end.
If you remember one thing: FOR repeats, IF decides, and a false IF skips the whole rest of its line.
FOR gives a variable a start value and an end value. The lines up to NEXT run once for each value. When the counter passes the end, BASIC carries on after NEXT. (See Figure 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. FOR sets the counter, NEXT adds the step and goes round again until the counter passes the end.

lesson.code:
10 for i=1 to 10
20 print i*7
30 next i

items: STEP changes the jump. STEP 2 gives 1, 3, 5. STEP -1 counts down, which is perfect for a rocket launch.

lesson.code:
10 for i=10 to 1 step -1
20 print i;
30 next i
40 print "liftoff"

items: IF tests a condition. When it is true, the rest of the line after THEN runs. When it is false, BASIC skips the whole rest of the line, including anything after a colon. This is a common surprise. (See Table 4.1 below.)

lesson.code:
10 input "a number";n
20 if n>=10 then print "big"
30 if n<10 then print "small"

lesson.title: Table 4.1. Tests you can use after IF
head: Symbol
Meaning
Example that is true

items: A colon puts several commands on one line. THEN followed by a number is a jump: IF A=0 THEN 100 is short for IF A=0 THEN GOTO 100. Inside BASIC, true is the number -1 and false is 0, so PRINT 5>3 prints -1.
Loops can sit inside loops. The outer loop picks a row, the inner loop does every column. Each FOR needs its own NEXT, inner one first.
Memory trick: FOR counts, IF chooses. FOR Counts round and round; IF Chooses, and a false IF skips the rest of the line.

chapters.title: Subroutines, DATA and arrays
summary: Bigger programs need tidy tools. GOSUB calls a helper block of lines and RETURN comes back. READ and DATA keep lists of numbers inside the program. DIM makes arrays, rows of numbered boxes.
RND gives random numbers for dice and games.
These tools are what you will use to store sprite pictures, tunes and game levels.

glossary.def: Jumps to a subroutine and remembers where to come back.
Goes back to the line after the GOSUB.
A line holding a list of values for READ.
Takes the next value from the DATA lines.
Starts reading the DATA from the beginning again.
Makes an array of a given size.
A random number from 0 up to (not including) 1.

keyPoints: GOSUB 100 runs the helper at line 100; RETURN comes back to just after the GOSUB.
Put END before your subroutines so the program does not fall into them.
READ takes the next item from DATA; RESTORE starts again.
DIM A(10) makes 11 boxes, A(0) to A(10).
INT(RND(1)*6)+1 rolls a dice from 1 to 6.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Decisions and loops:
• FOR I=1 TO 10 ... NEXT I repeats with I counting 1 to 10.
• STEP -1 counts down; STEP 2 counts in twos.
• IF test THEN action runs the action only when the test is true.
• Tests use = <> < > <= >=, combined with AND, OR, NOT.
• When IF is false, BASIC skips the rest of that line and goes to the next line.

ELI5. Imagine asking a helper to fetch something. You leave a note saying where you were, they go off, and when they come back they find your note and you carry on. And imagine a recipe card with a list of ingredients you read one at a time, and a row of numbered jars.

Now the real words. GOSUB jumps to a subroutine and RETURN comes back to the line after it; END stops the program from falling into the helpers by accident. READ takes the next value from DATA lines. DIM makes an array, a row of numbered boxes. RND gives random numbers, and INT(RND(1)*6)+1 rolls a dice.
Try it. Make a subroutine that draws a line of dashes and call it three times with GOSUB.
If you remember one thing: GOSUB goes, RETURN returns, END guards.
A subroutine is a helper you can call from anywhere. GOSUB jumps to it and RETURN brings you back to the line after the GOSUB, wherever that was. (See Figure 5.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.1. GOSUB jumps to the helper; RETURN comes back to the line after the call.

lesson.code:
10 gosub 100
20 print "title"
30 gosub 100
90 end
100 print "----------"
110 return

chapters.title: PEEK, POKE and the memory map
summary: Memory is a long street of 65536 numbered cells, each holding a number from 0 to 255. POKE writes into a cell; PEEK reads one.
Some cells are ordinary storage. Others belong to the chips: writing there changes colours, sounds and sprites. A map of the street tells you which is which.
With PEEK and POKE, BASIC can control every part of the machine.

glossary.def: One numbered place in memory that holds a byte.
A number from 0 to 255, made of 8 bits.
The number of a memory cell, from 0 to 65535.
Writes a byte into an address: POKE address,value.
Reads the byte at an address: PEEK(address).
A chip's control cell, such as 53280 for the border.
A list of what lives at which addresses.

keyPoints: POKE address,value writes; PEEK(address) reads.
Each cell holds 0 to 255; more gives ?ILLEGAL QUANTITY ERROR.
53280 is the border colour and 53281 the background; colours are 0 to 15.
The chips live at 53248 to 57343; 49152 to 53247 is free RAM.
Some registers use only some bits: AND 15 keeps the low four.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Subroutines, DATA and arrays:
• GOSUB 100 runs the helper at line 100; RETURN comes back to just after the GOSUB.
• Put END before your subroutines so the program does not fall into them.
• READ takes the next item from DATA; RESTORE starts again.
• DIM A(10) makes 11 boxes, A(0) to A(10).
• INT(RND(1)*6)+1 rolls a dice from 1 to 6.

ELI5. Imagine a long street of 65536 mailboxes. Most hold your things. Some are magic: put a number in the border mailbox and the edge of the screen changes colour. POKE is posting a number; PEEK is peeking in.

Now the real words. Memory has 65536 cells, each holding 0 to 255. POKE address,value writes a cell and PEEK(address) reads one. The memory map shows which addresses do what: the screen starts at 1024, free RAM at 49152, and the chips at 53248. 53280 is the border colour and 53281 the background, with 16 colours numbered 0 to 15.
Try it. Loop through all 16 colours on the border with a FOR loop and a short wait.
If you remember one thing: POKE puts and PEEK peeks; the chips are just special mailboxes.
Picture a street of 65536 mailboxes, numbered from 0 to 65535. Each box holds one number from 0 to 255, one byte. POKE puts a number in a box. PEEK looks inside.
Some stretches of the street are ordinary storage. Others are special: the screen, the BASIC language itself, and the control rooms of the chips. (See Figure 6.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.1. The memory map. The screen, your program, free RAM, the chips and the ROMs each have their own stretch of addresses.

items: The video chip starts at 53248. Its cell 53280 is the border colour and 53281 is the background. Any of the 16 colours can go in. (See Figure 6.2 below.) (See Table 6.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.2. The 16 colours. The same numbers work for the border, background, text and sprites.

items: Why does PEEK(53280) answer 254 rather than 14? The border register only uses its lowest four bits. The other four read back as 1s, which adds 240. AND 15 keeps just the low four bits: PEEK(53280) AND 15 gives the real colour number.

Bits are the eight on/off switches in a byte. From the right, they are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. 254 is all of them except the 1. Many chip registers pack several settings into one byte this way, one bit each. (See Table 6.2 below.)

items: Can a POKE do harm? Not to the computer. A wrong POKE into the wrong cell can crash the program or freeze the machine; Reset brings it back. Cells 49152 to 53247 are free RAM that BASIC never uses, a safe playground.
Memory trick: POKE puts, PEEK peeks. POKE Puts a number in a box; PEEK Peeks inside. Border 53280, background one more.

chapters.title: The screen is memory
summary: The text screen is 1000 memory cells: 40 columns by 25 rows, starting at address 1024. A second block of 1000 cells, starting at 55296, holds each cell's colour.
POKE a screen code into a cell and a character appears there, in any colour, without moving the cursor. PRINT can do colours too, with special control characters.
This is how most C64 games draw their playfields.

glossary.def: The 1000 cells from 1024 to 2023 that hold the characters on screen.
The 1000 cells from 55296 that hold each character's colour.
The number POKEd into screen memory for a character: A is 1, space is 32.
The C64's character code used by PRINT and CHR$: A is 65.
A PETSCII code that does something, such as 147 to clear the screen.
The flashing square where PRINT writes next.

keyPoints: Cell address = 1024 + row*40 + column; colour = 55296 + row*40 + column.
Screen codes (for POKE) differ from PETSCII codes (for PRINT): A is 1 vs 65.
CHR$(147) clears the screen; CHR$(19) moves the cursor home.
Colour control codes such as CHR$(28) change the text colour for PRINT.
Cell 646 holds the current text colour.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, PEEK, POKE and the memory map:
• POKE address,value writes; PEEK(address) reads.
• Each cell holds 0 to 255; more gives ?ILLEGAL QUANTITY ERROR.
• 53280 is the border colour and 53281 the background; colours are 0 to 15.
• The chips live at 53248 to 57343; 49152 to 53247 is free RAM.
• Some registers use only some bits: AND 15 keeps the low four.

ELI5. Imagine the screen is a grid of 1000 little windows, 40 across and 25 down. Each window has a number, and next to it a paint pot that decides its colour. Put a letter number in a window and a colour in its pot and it lights up.

Now the real words. Screen memory starts at 1024, and a cell's address is 1024 + row*40 + column. Colour RAM starts at 55296 with the same layout. POKE uses screen codes (A is 1) while PRINT uses PETSCII (A is 65). PRINT CHR$(147) clears the screen, and colour codes such as CHR$(28) switch the text colour.
Try it. Put a star at row 12, column 20 by working out the address, and give it a colour.
If you remember one thing: cell = 1024 + row times 40 + column, and always set the colour too.

The screen you see is a window onto memory. The 40 by 25 grid of character cells is stored in 1000 cells starting at 1024. Change a cell and the picture changes on the next frame. (See Figure 7.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.1. Each character cell has an address. Rows are 40 cells apart.

items: To find the cell for a row and column, start at 1024, add 40 for each row down, then add the column. Rows and columns count from 0. Row 12, column 20 is 1024 + 480 + 20 = 1524, close to the middle.
Colour RAM works the same way from 55296. Without a colour POKE, a new character may be the same colour as the background and stay invisible, so always set both.

Here is the catch: the number for a letter depends on how you put it there. POKE uses screen codes, where @ is 0, A is 1 and space is 32. PRINT and CHR$ use PETSCII, where A is 65, as in ASCII. (See Table 7.1 below.)

head: Character
Screen code (POKE)
PETSCII (PRINT, CHR$)

items: PRINT also understands control characters. Some move the cursor, some change the colour of everything printed after them. CHR$(147) clears the screen and puts the cursor in the top left, the first line of almost every program. (See Table 7.2 below.)

lesson.code: 10 print chr$(147);chr$(28);"red";chr$(5);" and white"

items: On a real C64 you can type these codes inside quotes with the cursor and colour keys; they show as reversed symbols. In the lab, CHR$ is clearer and easier to read. POKE 646,1 also sets the text colour, which PRINT then uses.
Memory trick: Ten-twenty-four plus forty a row. Screen starts at 1024, plus 40 for every row, plus the column; colour lives at 55296.

chapters.title: Sprites
summary: A sprite is a small picture, 24 by 21 dots, that the video chip draws on top of the screen. You can move it anywhere by changing two numbers, without redrawing anything.
The C64 has eight sprites. Each needs a picture (63 bytes), a pointer to that picture, a position, a colour and an on switch.
Sprites are the players, enemies and bullets of nearly every C64 game.

glossary.def: A 24 by 21 dot picture the VIC-II draws over the screen.
The cell (2040 to 2047) that says which 64-byte block holds a sprite's picture.
A 64-byte chunk of memory; block 13 starts at 13*64 = 832.
V+21 (53269): one bit per sprite switches it on.
V+23 and V+29 double a sprite's height and width.
Short for 53248, the first VIC-II register.

keyPoints: A sprite is 63 bytes: 21 rows of 3 bytes, 8 dots per byte.
POKE 2040,13 points sprite 0 at block 13 (cells 832 to 894).
V=53248: X is V, Y is V+1, colour is V+39, on/off is V+21.
Each sprite has one bit in V+21: sprite 0 is 1, sprite 1 is 2, sprite 2 is 4.
V+23 doubles height, V+29 doubles width.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, The screen is memory:
• Cell address = 1024 + row*40 + column; colour = 55296 + row*40 + column.
• Screen codes (for POKE) differ from PETSCII codes (for PRINT): A is 1 vs 65.
• CHR$(147) clears the screen; CHR$(19) moves the cursor home.
• Colour control codes such as CHR$(28) change the text colour for PRINT.
• Cell 646 holds the current text colour.

ELI5. Imagine a sticker that you can slide around a picture without smudging it. You draw it on a tiny grid of dots, tell the painter which page of your notebook it is on, where to put it, what colour it is, and then say go.

Now the real words. A sprite is 24 by 21 dots, stored in 63 bytes, three per row. The data goes in a 64-byte block such as 832, and pointer 2040 holds the block number (13). With V=53248, V and V+1 are the position, V+39 the colour, and V+21 switches sprites on, one bit each. V+23 and V+29 make it double size.
Try it. Read the ball DATA into 832, point 2040 at 13, set a position and colour, switch it on, and slide it across with a loop.
If you remember one thing: data, pointer, place, paint, power on.

A sprite is like a sticker that slides over the picture. The VIC-II draws it on top of the text in hardware, so moving it costs one POKE. The picture itself is a grid of 24 by 21 dots. Each row is three bytes, and each bit of a byte is one dot: 1 is coloured, 0 is see-through.
(See Figure 8.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.1. A sprite is 63 bytes. Each byte is eight dots; three bytes make one 24-dot row.

items: To work out a byte, add up the values of its coloured dots: from the left they are worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. A full row of eight is 255; the middle six dots are 64+32+16+8+4+2 = 126.

The 63 bytes have to live in memory somewhere the VIC-II can see, in a 64-byte block. Blocks 13, 14 and 15 (cells 832 to 1023) are free and safe. The sprite pointer for sprite 0, at cell 2040, holds the block number.

lesson.code:
10 v=53248
20 for i=0 to 62:read a:poke 832+i,a:next
30 poke 2040,13
40 poke v,160:poke v+1,120
50 poke v+39,7
60 poke v+21,1
100 data 0,126,0,1,255,128,3,255,192 ...and so on: 63 numbers

items: V is short for 53248, where the VIC-II starts. Most sprite settings are V plus a small number, so the program stays readable. (See Table 8.1 below.)

Address
What it does
rows: X and Y for sprites 1 to 7, in pairs
ninth X bit (to go past 255) for each sprite

items: Each register like V+21 has one bit for each of the eight sprites. Sprite 0 is worth 1, sprite 1 is 2, sprite 2 is 4, up to sprite 7, which is 128. To switch on sprites 0 and 1, POKE V+21,3.

Positions are counted in dots. X runs from 0 to 255 in V, and the ninth bit in V+16 adds 256 for the right edge. The visible screen starts at about X 24 and Y 50, so a sprite at 0,0 hides in the border.
To move a sprite, change its X or Y in a loop. The sprite glides because the VIC-II redraws it 50 times a second at the new position.

items: Memory trick: Data, point, place, paint, power. Sprite steps: Data at 832, Pointer 2040, Place with V and V+1, Paint with V+39, Power on with V+21.

chapters.title: Sound with the SID
summary: The SID chip has three voices. Each voice has a pitch, a waveform and an envelope that shapes how the note swells and fades. A master volume controls them all.
Playing a note is a handful of POKEs: volume, envelope, pitch, then a waveform with the gate bit to start it.
The SID's rich sound is a big part of why C64 music is still loved.

glossary.def: Sound Interface Device, the C64's sound chip.
One of the SID's three independent sound makers.
The shape of the sound wave: triangle, sawtooth, pulse or noise.
Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release: how a note's loudness changes.
Bit 0 of the control register: on starts the note, off starts the release.
Short for 54272, the first SID register.

keyPoints: Set the volume first: POKE S+24,15.
S+5 is attack*16+decay; S+6 is sustain*16+release.
S+1 and S are the pitch (high and low byte).
S+4 picks the waveform: 16 triangle, 32 saw, 64 pulse, 128 noise; add 1 to open the gate.
Writing the waveform without the 1 closes the gate and the note fades.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Sprites:
• A sprite is 63 bytes: 21 rows of 3 bytes, 8 dots per byte.
• POKE 2040,13 points sprite 0 at block 13 (cells 832 to 894).
• V=53248: X is V, Y is V+1, colour is V+39, on/off is V+21.
• Each sprite has one bit in V+21: sprite 0 is 1, sprite 1 is 2, sprite 2 is 4.
• V+23 doubles height, V+29 doubles width.

ELI5. Imagine three singers. You tell them how loud the room is, how each note should swell and fade, how high to sing and with what kind of voice. Then you open the door and they start singing, and when you close it, they fade away.

Now the real words. The SID starts at S=54272. S+24 is the volume, S+5 and S+6 are the envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release), S+1 and S are the pitch, and S+4 picks the waveform: 16 triangle, 32 sawtooth, 64 pulse, 128 noise. Adding 1 opens the gate and starts the note; writing it without the 1 lets the note fade.
Try it. Play one note with volume 15, a triangle wave and the gate open, then close the gate after a wait.
If you remember one thing: volume, envelope, pitch, then open the gate.
Think of each voice as a singer. You tell it how loud to be overall, how the note should swell and fade, how high to sing, and with what kind of voice. Then you open the gate and it starts.

Line 20 sets the master volume to the maximum, 15. Line 30 sets the envelope. Line 40 sets the pitch. Line 50 chooses a triangle wave (16) and adds 1 to open the gate. The note sounds until you close the gate.

The envelope has four parts. Attack is how fast the note rises, decay how fast it falls to the sustain level, sustain is the level it holds while the gate is open, and release is how fast it fades after the gate closes. (See Figure 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.1. The ADSR envelope. The gate opens the note; closing it starts the release.

items: Each envelope value is 0 to 15. Two values share one cell: the first is multiplied by 16. So POKE S+5,9 means attack 0 (instant) and decay 9; POKE S+6,240 means sustain 15 (full) and release 0.
The waveform gives each voice its colour. (See Figure 9.2 below.) (See Table 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.2. The four waveforms. Add 1 for the gate.

items: Pitch is a 16-bit number split across two cells: high byte times 256 plus low byte. Bigger numbers mean higher notes; doubling the number goes up an octave. A melody is just a list of pitch pairs in DATA lines, read in a loop, with a short wait and a gate off between notes.

20 for n=1 to 4
30 read h,l:poke s+1,h:poke s,l
40 poke s+4,17:for d=1 to 150:next:poke s+4,16
50 next
70 data 34,75,38,126,43,52,45,198

items: The waits in BASIC are rough; the speed depends on how busy the program is. Later chapters show how machine code and interrupts keep perfect time, which is how real C64 music players work.

summary: A joystick is five switches: four directions and fire. The C64 reads them through CIA 1, at 56320 for port 2 and 56321 for port 1.
A pressed switch reads as 0, not 1. AND picks out one switch at a time.
GET reads the keyboard without stopping the program, which is what games need.

glossary.def: One of the two 9-pin joystick sockets.
A switch that reads 0 when pressed and 1 when released.
Using AND with a bit value to test one bit.
Reads one key if one is waiting, otherwise gives an empty string.
Up to 10 key presses the C64 remembers until read.

keyPoints: Port 2 is PEEK(56320); port 1 is PEEK(56321).
Up 1, down 2, left 4, right 8, fire 16.
Pressed reads 0: test with IF (J AND 16)=0 THEN.
GET A$ never waits; loop until A$ is not empty.
Port 1 shares wires with the keyboard, so games prefer port 2.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Sound with the SID:
• Set the volume first: POKE S+24,15.
• S+5 is attack*16+decay; S+6 is sustain*16+release.
• S+1 and S are the pitch (high and low byte).
• S+4 picks the waveform: 16 triangle, 32 saw, 64 pulse, 128 noise; add 1 to open the gate.
• Writing the waveform without the 1 closes the gate and the note fades.
ELI5. Imagine five light switches that are on when nobody touches them, and go off when you press them. To check one switch, you cover the others with your hand and look only at that one.

Now the real words. A joystick is five switches: up 1, down 2, left 4, right 8 and fire 16. PEEK(56320) reads port 2 and PEEK(56321) port 1. A pressed switch reads 0, so you test it with IF (J AND 16)=0. GET reads a key without stopping the program; if no key is waiting it gives an empty string.
Try it. Print FIRE! whenever fire is pressed, and use the pad under the screen to test it.
If you remember one thing: pressed is zero, and AND picks out one switch.

Inside a joystick are five switches. Each one connects one wire to ground when you press it. The CIA chip reads those wires as bits of one byte. Because pressing connects the wire to ground, a pressed switch reads as 0. (See Figure 10.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.1. Five switches, one bit each. Pressed is 0, so the number goes down when you push.

lesson.code:
10 print peek(56320)
20 goto 10

items: With nothing pressed this prints 127. Hold fire and it drops to 111, because bit 4 (worth 16) went to 0. To test one switch on its own, AND the reading with its value. If the answer is 0, that switch is pressed. (See Table 10.1 below.)

lesson.code:
10 j=peek(56320)
20 if (j and 16)=0 then print "fire!"
30 if (j and 4)=0 then print "left"
40 goto 10

items: Several switches can be pressed at once, such as up and fire; each bit is tested on its own. Diagonals are simply two directions together.
For the keyboard, INPUT stops the whole program until RETURN, which is no good for a game. GET looks for one key and carries on at once. If nothing was pressed, the string is empty.

lesson.code:
10 get a$
20 if a$="" then 10
30 print "you pressed ";a$

items: Keys pressed while the program is busy wait in a 10-key buffer. POKE 198,0 empties it, which is handy before asking a question so old presses do not leak in. In the lab, tap the screen to give the C64 the keyboard, and use the pad under the screen for the joystick.
Memory trick: Pressed is zero. On the joystick, Pressed is Zero: up 1, down 2, left 4, right 8, fire 16.

chapters.title: The C64's ports

maps.title: Ports
links: User port | lines | PB0 to PB7

summary: The C64 talks to the world through its sockets, called ports: two control ports, the user port, the cassette port, the serial port for disk drives and printers, the expansion port for cartridges, and video and power sockets.
Each port is wired to a chip, and so it shows up as memory cells you can PEEK and POKE. The user port gives you eight lines you can switch on and off yourself.
This chapter has a map of the ports, a table of pins for each, and a lab that drives the user port lines.

glossary.def: A socket on the computer that connects to the outside world.
One wire contact in a port.
A 24-contact edge connector with eight programmable data lines.
A cell that says which lines are inputs (0) and which are outputs (1).
The 6-pin round socket for disk drives and printers.
The cartridge slot: the whole bus brought out to a connector.
A 0 to 5 volt logic signal: about 0 V is a 0, about 5 V is a 1.

keyPoints: Control ports 1 and 2 are 9-pin sockets read at 56321 and 56320.
The user port lines PB0-PB7 are cell 56577; 56579 sets them as outputs (1) or inputs (0).
The serial port connects disk drives (device 8 and up) and printers (device 4).
The cassette port is for the Datassette tape drive (device 1).
Every line is a 5 V logic signal: protect it with a resistor and never connect mains or higher voltages.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Joystick and keyboard:
• Port 2 is PEEK(56320); port 1 is PEEK(56321).
• Up 1, down 2, left 4, right 8, fire 16.
• Pressed reads 0: test with IF (J AND 16)=0 THEN.
• GET A$ never waits; loop until A$ is not empty.
• Port 1 shares wires with the keyboard, so games prefer port 2.

ELI5. Imagine a house with different doors: two small ones for game controllers, a big back door for building your own gadgets, a door for the tape player, a door for the disk drive, and a slot for cartridges. Each door is connected to one of the helpers inside.

Now the real words. The control ports are 9-pin sockets: pins 1 to 4 are directions, 6 is fire, 7 is +5 V and 8 is ground. The user port is an edge of the circuit board with eight lines, PB0 to PB7: POKE 56579,255 makes them outputs and POKE 56577 sets them on or off. The serial port talks to disk drives and printers, the cassette port to the tape drive, and the expansion port takes cartridges. All lines are 5 volt logic signals.
Try it. Make all user port lines outputs and run a single lit line from PB0 to PB7, doubling the value each time.
If you remember one thing: each port is wired to a chip, so it is just a few memory cells, and it only likes gentle 5 volt signals.
Look around a C64 and you find sockets on the side and along the back. Each one has a job, and behind each one is a chip you already know. (See Figure 11.1 below.) (See Table 11.1 below.)

The user port is the hobbyist's favourite. It is not a socket but an edge of the main circuit board with 12 contacts on top and 12 underneath. The eight lines PB0 to PB7 on the bottom row are yours to control. (See Figure 11.3 below.) (See Table 11.3 below.)

chapters.title: Build a small game
summary: Now you put it all together: a sprite you steer with the joystick, a score that goes up when you press fire, and a sound and a flash for each point.
Every game is the same loop: read the controls, move things, apply the rules, show the result, repeat.
You build the game in three small steps, testing after each one.

glossary.def: The repeating cycle of read, move, rules, show.
The variables that describe the game right now: position, score, lives.
Reacting when a button is newly pressed, not while it is held.
Keeping a position inside the screen.
Sound, flashes and messages that tell the player something happened.

keyPoints: A game is one loop: read, move, rules, show.
Keep the state in a few variables such as X and SC.
Check the edges: only move if X is inside the allowed range.
Count a press once by remembering whether fire was already down.
Put repeated effects (sound, flash) in a subroutine.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, The C64's ports:
• Control ports 1 and 2 are 9-pin sockets read at 56321 and 56320.
• The user port lines PB0-PB7 are cell 56577; 56579 sets them as outputs (1) or inputs (0).
• The serial port connects disk drives (device 8 and up) and printers (device 4).
• The cassette port is for the Datassette tape drive (device 1).
• Every line is a 5 V logic signal: protect it with a resistor and never connect mains or higher voltages.
ELI5. Imagine a flip book. On each page you look at the controller, move the hero a little, check if anything happened, and draw the picture. Flip through fast and it moves.

Now the real words. Every game is one loop: read the controls, move things, apply the rules, show the result, and go round again. The state lives in variables such as X for position and SC for score. A bounds check keeps the sprite on screen, and remembering whether fire was already down makes one press count once. Sound and flashes go in a subroutine.
Try it. Add steering, then scoring, then a blip with a border flash, testing after each step.
If you remember one thing: read, move, rules, show, and repeat.

Every game, from Pong to the biggest C64 hits, repeats one loop. Read the controls. Move the things that move. Apply the rules: scores, hits, lives. Show the result with sprites and sound. Then go round again, many times a second. (See Figure 12.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 12.1. The game loop. Each trip round is one moment of the game.

items: Step one: steering. The sprite's X position is in a variable, X. Each trip round the loop reads the joystick and changes X a little. A bounds check stops the sprite leaving the screen.

lesson.code:
40 j=peek(56320)
50 if (j and 4)=0 and x>30 then x=x-6
60 if (j and 8)=0 and x<250 then x=x+6
70 poke v,x
90 goto 40

items: Step two: scoring. If the score went up on every trip while fire is held, one press would score dozens of points. The trick is to remember whether fire was already down, in a variable F, and only score when it goes from up to down.

lesson.code:
50 if (j and 16)<>0 then f=0
60 if (j and 16)=0 and f=0 then f=1:sc=sc+1:print chr$(19);"score";sc

items: CHR$(19) moves the cursor home without clearing, so the score is redrawn in the same place at the top.
Step three: feedback. A short blip and a border flash make each point feel real. Because it may happen from several places, it goes in a subroutine. (See Table 12.1 below.)

lesson.code:
200 poke 53280,1:poke s+4,33:for d=1 to 30:next
210 poke s+4,32:poke 53280,14:return

chapters.title: First machine code
summary: Machine code is the processor's own language: each instruction is one to three bytes. Assembly language writes those instructions as short words such as LDA and STA, and an assembler turns them into bytes.
Machine code runs hundreds of times faster than BASIC. It is how C64 games, music players and demos were written.
You start gently: load a number, store it somewhere, return to BASIC.

glossary.def: The bytes the processor runs directly.
A readable way of writing machine code, one instruction per line.
The tool that turns assembly text into bytes.
A tiny one-byte store inside the processor: A, X or Y.
Base 16, written with a $: $C000 is 49152, $D020 is 53280.
A # before a number means the number itself: LDA #2.
The BASIC command that starts machine code at an address.

keyPoints: LDA #n loads the number n into A; STA addr stores A into a cell.
# means the number itself; without # it means the cell at that address.
*=$C000 puts the code at 49152; SYS 49152 runs it.
RTS returns to BASIC; forget it and the C64 runs into garbage.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Build a small game:
• A game is one loop: read, move, rules, show.
• Keep the state in a few variables such as X and SC.
• Check the edges: only move if X is inside the allowed range.
• Count a press once by remembering whether fire was already down.
• Put repeated effects (sound, flash) in a subroutine.
ELI5. Imagine talking to the brain in its own tiny language. It has three pockets, A, X and Y. You say: put 2 in pocket A, now put whatever is in pocket A into the border mailbox, now go back home.

Now the real words. Machine code is the processor's own language, written in assembly as short words. LDA #2 loads the number 2 into A, STA $D020 stores A into the border cell, and RTS returns to BASIC. The $ means hexadecimal, so $D020 is 53280 and $C000 is 49152. The lab assembles your text, puts it at $C000 and starts it with SYS 49152.
Try it. Make the border red and the background black in assembly.
If you remember one thing: load, store, return, and don't forget the RTS.

The 6510 has three tiny pockets called registers: A, X and Y. Each holds one byte. Almost everything goes through A, the accumulator: you load a number into it, then store it somewhere. (See Figure 13.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 13.1. The 6510's registers and flags. A does the work; X and Y count; flags remember results.

items: Here is POKE 53280,2 written in assembly:

lesson.code:
*=$C000
      lda #2
      sta $d020
      rts

items: Line by line: *=$C000 tells the assembler to put the code at address $C000. LDA #2 loads the number 2 into A. STA $D020 stores A into cell $D020, the border. RTS (return from subroutine) goes back to whoever called the code, here BASIC.

Two new habits. First, addresses are usually written in hexadecimal, base 16, marked with $. Hex lines up neatly with bytes: two hex digits are exactly one byte. Second, the # matters: LDA #2 loads the number 2, while LDA 2 loads whatever is in cell 2. (See Table 13.1 below.)

chapters.title: Loops and the KERNAL

maps.title: Loops
links: X register | changed by | INX DEX

summary: Machine code loops use a counter register, usually X, and a branch: add one, compare, and jump back while not finished.
Indexed addressing, such as STA $0400,X, lets one instruction reach a whole row of cells.
The KERNAL is the C64's built-in library. JSR calls its routines, such as $FFD2 to print a character.

glossary.def: Add one to X / take one from X.
Compare X with a value and set the flags.
Branch if not equal / if equal (tests the Z flag).
addr,X means the cell at addr plus X.
A name for an address, such as loop:, that branches can jump to.
Jump to subroutine: like GOSUB, RTS comes back.
The C64's operating system routines in ROM, called through a jump table at the top of memory.

keyPoints: A loop: LDX #0, body, INX, CPX #n, BNE back to the label.
STA $0400,X stores into 1024+X, so X walks along the row.
The Z flag is set when a result or comparison is equal; BNE jumps while it is not.
JSR $FFD2 prints the character code in A (CHROUT).
A zero byte at the end of a message tells a print loop where to stop.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, First machine code:
• LDA #n loads the number n into A; STA addr stores A into a cell.
• # means the number itself; without # it means the cell at that address.
• *=$C000 puts the code at 49152; SYS 49152 runs it.
• RTS returns to BASIC; forget it and the C64 runs into garbage.

ELI5. Imagine putting stickers along a row of boxes. You keep a finger counting: stick one, move your finger along, check if you are at the end, and if not, go again. And imagine a toolbox full of ready-made tools you can borrow by calling their names.

Now the real words. A loop in assembly uses X as the counter: STA $0400,X stores into the cell at $0400 plus X, INX adds one, CPX #40 compares, and BNE jumps back while they are not equal. The KERNAL is the C64's built-in toolbox; JSR $FFD2 calls CHROUT, which prints the character in A. A zero byte marks the end of a message.
Try it. Fill the whole top row with hearts, then print a message with a loop that stops at the zero byte.
If you remember one thing: count, compare, branch, and JSR to borrow the KERNAL's tools.
BASIC's FOR loop becomes four ideas in assembly: set a counter, do the work, change the counter, and branch back if not finished. (See Figure 14.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 14.1. A counting loop: X walks from 0 to 39 and BNE jumps back until it reaches 40.

lesson.code:
*=$C000
      ldx #0
      lda #83
loop: sta $0400,x
      inx
      cpx #40
      bne loop
      rts

items: loop: is a label, a name for the address of the next instruction. STA $0400,X stores A into $0400 plus X. INX adds one to X. CPX #40 compares X with 40 and sets the Z (zero) flag if they are equal. BNE loop branches back while Z is not set.
After forty trips X is 40 and the code falls through to RTS. (See Table 14.1 below.)

summary: The video chip draws the picture line by line, 50 times a second. Machine code is fast enough to change colours while a single picture is being drawn, which creates stripes and bars.
The raster register $D012 tells you which line is being drawn. An interrupt lets the video chip call your code at a chosen line, every frame, while BASIC keeps running.
Interrupts are how C64 music players, smooth scrolling and split screens work.

glossary.def: The line of the picture being drawn right now, in $D012.
One full picture: 312 lines on a PAL C64, about 50 per second.
One tick of the 1 MHz clock; a line takes 63 cycles on PAL.
A signal that pauses the program, runs a handler, and resumes.
A cell holding the address to jump to, such as $0314 for the IRQ handler.
Turn interrupts off / back on.
Return from interrupt.

keyPoints: A PAL frame is 312 lines of 63 cycles: 19656 cycles, about 50 frames a second.
$D012 is the current raster line; waiting for it to change syncs you to the beam.
INC $D020 in a tight loop changes the border many times per frame: stripes.
A raster interrupt: SEI, point $0314/$0315 at the handler, enable in $D01A, pick a line in $D012, CLI.
The handler must acknowledge with $D019, or it is called again straight away.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Loops and the KERNAL:
• A loop: LDX #0, body, INX, CPX #n, BNE back to the label.
• STA $0400,X stores into 1024+X, so X walks along the row.
• The Z flag is set when a result or comparison is equal; BNE jumps while it is not.
• JSR $FFD2 prints the character code in A (CHROUT).
• A zero byte at the end of a message tells a print loop where to stop.

ELI5. Imagine the picture on the screen is painted by a tiny brush that sweeps line by line, top to bottom, fifty times a second. If you change the paint while it is halfway down, only the bottom half changes. An interrupt is a tap on the shoulder when the brush reaches a line you chose.

Now the real words. A PAL frame has 312 lines of 63 cycles. $D012 holds the line being drawn. Changing the border in a tight loop gives stripes; waiting for the line to change gives steady bars. A raster interrupt needs SEI, the handler address in $0314 and $0315, the raster enable in $D01A, a line in $D012, and CLI. The handler acknowledges in $D019 and ends with RTI.
Try it. Make raster bars, then set up an interrupt that counts frames in a memory cell while BASIC keeps working.
If you remember one thing: the screen is drawn line by line, and an interrupt lets you act at exactly the right moment.

The picture is not drawn all at once. A beam sweeps across and down, line by line, 312 lines for each picture on a PAL C64, 50 pictures a second. The VIC-II reads the colour registers as it goes, so if you change the border halfway down, only the lower half changes. (See Figure 15.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 15.1. The raster beam. A raster interrupt fires when the beam reaches a chosen line.

lesson.code:
*=$C000
loop: inc $d020
      jmp loop

items: This tiny loop adds one to the border colour about every 9 cycles. The beam moves 8 dots per cycle, so the border changes every few dozen dots: a mess of colour stripes. It never returns to BASIC; press RUN/STOP and RESTORE on a real C64, or Reset in the lab.
Waiting for $D012 to change before each colour step makes one colour per raster line instead: steady horizontal bars. (See Table 15.1 below.)

lesson.code:
loop: lda $d012
wait: cmp $d012
      beq wait
      sta $d020
      jmp loop

items: Busy loops take over the whole machine. An interrupt is politer: it is a tap on the shoulder. When the beam reaches your chosen line, the processor finishes its current instruction, saves where it was, runs your handler, and goes back. BASIC never notices.

Setting one up takes a few steps: switch interrupts off with SEI so nothing fires half-way, store the handler's address in the vector at $0314 and $0315, turn off the CIA timer interrupt, enable the raster interrupt in $D01A, choose the line in $D012, and switch interrupts back on with CLI.
(See Table 15.2 below.)

items: The handler does its job, then acknowledges the interrupt by writing to $D019. Without that, the VIC-II keeps signalling and the handler runs forever. It ends by restoring the registers the KERNAL saved and executing RTI.

lesson.code:
irq:  inc $d020     ; the job
      lda #$ff
      sta $d019     ; acknowledge
      pla
      tay
      pla
      tax
      pla
      rti

items: This is the heartbeat of most C64 software: once per frame, the handler moves sprites, plays the next step of the music and updates the score, perfectly on time.
Memory trick: Point, enable, choose, acknowledge. Interrupts: Point $0314 at the handler, Enable in $D01A, Choose the line in $D012, Acknowledge in $D019.

summary: C sits between BASIC and assembly: you write readable code with variables, loops and functions, and a compiler turns it into fast machine code.
cc65 is a free C compiler for the 6502 family. In the lab, cc65, its assembler ca65 and its linker ld65 run inside the app, and the result runs on the same C64.
You learn the shape of a C program, types, loops, functions, and PEEK and POKE from C.

glossary.def: A compiled programming language from 1972, still everywhere today.
A program that turns source code into machine code before it runs.
A free C compiler (and toolchain) for 6502 computers including the C64.
What a variable can hold: unsigned char is 0 to 255, int is -32768 to 32767.
A named block of code with inputs and an optional result; C's subroutine.
A file included with #include that declares ready-made functions, such as stdio.h.
The C64 program file format: two address bytes, then the program.

keyPoints: A C program starts in int main(void) { ... }.
Every variable has a type; unsigned char (0-255) is the fastest on the 6510.
for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { ... } is BASIC's FOR...NEXT.
#include <peekpoke.h> gives POKE(addr, v) and PEEK(addr).
cc65 compiles, ca65 assembles, ld65 links: the result is a PRG that BASIC RUNs.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Timing and interrupts:
• A PAL frame is 312 lines of 63 cycles: 19656 cycles, about 50 frames a second.
• $D012 is the current raster line; waiting for it to change syncs you to the beam.
• INC $D020 in a tight loop changes the border many times per frame: stripes.
• A raster interrupt: SEI, point $0314/$0315 at the handler, enable in $D01A, pick a line in $D012, CLI.
• The handler must acknowledge with $D019, or it is called again straight away.

ELI5. Imagine writing a letter in friendly words and handing it to a translator, who rewrites the whole thing in the brain's tiny language before anyone reads it. The translated version runs very fast.

Now the real words. C is a compiled language. cc65 compiles your C to assembly, ca65 assembles it and ld65 links it with the C library into a .prg file that the C64 runs. A program starts in int main(void). Variables need types; unsigned char (0 to 255) is fastest on the 6510. for loops count, == tests equality, and peekpoke.h gives POKE and PEEK.
Try it. Print HELLO FROM C, then print the seven times table with a for loop.
If you remember one thing: compile, assemble, link, and prefer unsigned char.

BASIC is interpreted: each line is read and worked out every time it runs, which is slow. C is compiled: a compiler translates the whole program into machine code once, before it runs. You get readable code and most of the speed of assembly. (See Figure 16.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 16.1. The cc65 toolchain. In the lab all three tools run inside the app.

items: #include <stdio.h> brings in the standard input and output functions, such as printf. main is where the program starts. The curly braces hold its body. Each statement ends with a semicolon. \n inside the text means new line.
In cc65, small letters in your text show as capitals on the C64's normal screen.

C variables must be declared with a type before use. On the 6510, which works one byte at a time, small types are much faster, so prefer unsigned char where the value fits in 0 to 255. (See Table 16.1 below.)
The for line has three parts: start (i = 1), keep going while (i <= 10), and step (i++ adds one). %u in printf is a hole for an unsigned number. (See Table 16.2 below.)

items: Note the double equals: in C, a = 5 sets a, while a == 5 tests it. Mixing them up is the classic C bug. The U after a number such as 53280U says it is unsigned, which keeps cc65 from warning about big addresses.
Functions are C's subroutines, but they can take inputs and give back a result. void means no result.

When you press Run in the lab, cc65 turns the C into assembly, ca65 assembles it, and ld65 links it with the C library into a PRG that starts with a tiny BASIC line, so the C64 RUNs it like any program. If the compiler finds a mistake, its message names the line.

summary: The chips do not know which language wrote to them. Every register from the BASIC chapters works the same from C, through POKE and PEEK.
C is fast enough to move sprites smoothly, once per frame, by waiting for the raster line just as the assembly chapter did.
You set up a sprite, play a note, steer with the joystick and use a table of numbers for smooth motion.

glossary.def: A chip's control cell, the same in every language.
C's AND for testing bits: (j & 16) == 0 means fire is pressed.
for (;;) { ... } runs forever, the game loop in C.
An array of precomputed numbers, such as the points of a wave.
Waiting for a raster line so work happens once per picture.

keyPoints: Sprites from C: same 63 bytes at 832, pointer 2040, X/Y at 53248/53249, colour 53287, on 53269.
Sound from C: volume 54296, envelope 54277/54278, pitch 54273/54272, control 54276.
Joystick from C: j = PEEK(56320U); if ((j & 8) == 0) moves right.
while (PEEK(53266U) != 250); waits for raster line 250: one step per frame.
A lookup table makes smooth motion without slow maths.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, C with cc65:
• A C program starts in int main(void) { ... }.
• Every variable has a type; unsigned char (0-255) is the fastest on the 6510.
• for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { ... } is BASIC's FOR...NEXT.
• #include <peekpoke.h> gives POKE(addr, v) and PEEK(addr).
• cc65 compiles, ca65 assembles, ld65 links: the result is a PRG that BASIC RUNs.

ELI5. Imagine the helpers inside the C64 only read numbers in their mailboxes. They don't care if the note was written in BASIC, in assembly or in C. And imagine a cheat sheet of answers worked out in advance, so you don't have to do hard sums while the game is running.

Now the real words. The registers are the same from every language: POKE(53269U, 1) switches a sprite on just like POKE 53269,1. (j & 8) == 0 tests the joystick. for (;;) loops forever, and waiting for raster line 250 moves things once per frame. A lookup table of precomputed numbers makes smooth curves without slow maths.
Try it. Steer a sprite with the joystick from C, then make it swing by doubling the numbers in the wave table.
If you remember one thing: the chips only see cells and numbers, so any language can drive them.

Everything you learned about the chips carries over. In BASIC you wrote POKE 53269,1. In C you write POKE(53269U, 1);. The VIC-II sees the same number in the same cell. (See Figure 17.1 below.) (See Table 17.1 below.)

items: C's & is a bitwise AND, like BASIC's AND on numbers. Testing a joystick switch reads exactly as before, with C's == for the comparison.

for (;;) loops forever. && means both conditions must be true. The last line waits until the raster beam reaches line 250, near the bottom of the picture. That ties the loop to the frame rate: exactly one step per picture, 50 a second, so movement is smooth and the same speed on every run.
Smooth curved motion needs sine values, but calculating sines on a 1 MHz computer is slow. The classic trick is a lookup table: work the numbers out once, store them in an array, and step through it.

& 15 keeps k between 0 and 15, so the table repeats forever without an if. Demos and games are full of tables like this: for movement, colours, music and even pre-drawn graphics. (See Table 17.2 below.)

chapters.title: Saving your work: tape and disk
summary: When you switch a C64 off, memory is wiped. To keep programs you save them to cassette tape or floppy disk, and LOAD them back later.
Each storage device has a number: 1 for tape, 8 for the first disk drive. Disks have a directory you can list.
This last chapter explains the commands, the file types and how emulators store tapes and disks as files today.

keyPoints: SAVE "NAME",8 saves the BASIC program to disk; LOAD "NAME",8 loads it.
LOAD "$",8 then LIST shows the disk directory (it replaces the program in memory).

Device 1 is tape, 8 the first disk drive, 4 the printer.

ELI5. Imagine the C64 forgets everything when you turn it off, like a whiteboard wiped clean. To keep your work, you copy it onto a tape, like recording a song, or onto a disk, like a record with a list of songs in the middle.

Now the real words. SAVE "NAME",8 saves to disk and LOAD "NAME",8 loads it back. LOAD "$",8 then LIST shows the directory. Device 1 is tape, 4 the printer and 8 the first disk drive. A 1541 disk has 35 tracks with the directory on track 18. Emulators keep disks and tapes as .d64, .tap and .prg files.

If you remember one thing: 8 for disk, 1 for tape, and save before you switch off.
A program in memory lasts only until the power goes off. Saving copies it to a tape or disk; loading copies it back. The commands are short and take a device number after the name.

sandbox.intro: A scripted lookup, not a real machine. Try: start, basic, screen, colours, sprite, sound, joy, ports, asm, kernal, irq, c, disk, help

out: colours    0 black 1 white 2 red 3 cyan 4 purple 5 green 6 blue 7 yello
ports      control ports: 9-pin, pins 1-4 directions, 6 fire, 7 +5V, 8
for i=1 to 10 step 1 ... next   if a=1 then ...
gosub 100 ... return   read/data   dim a(10)   int(rnd(1)*6)+1
chr$(147) clear, chr$(19) home, chr$(28) red
0 black 1 white 2 red 3 cyan 4 purple 5 green 6 blue 7 yellow
8 orange 9 brown 10 light red 11 dark grey 12 grey 13 light green 14 light blue 15 light grey
poke v,x : poke v+1,y : poke v+39,colour : poke v+21,1
v+23 double height, v+29 double width
poke s+5,9:poke s+6,240 (envelope), poke s+1,34:poke s,75 (pitch)
poke s+4,17 start (triangle+gate), poke s+4,16 stop
up 1 down 2 left 4 right 8 fire 16; pressed = 0
control ports: 9-pin, pins 1-4 directions, 6 fire, 7 +5V, 8 ground
user port: poke 56579,255 outputs, poke 56577,v sets PB0-PB7
serial: disk device 8, printer 4; cassette: device 1
ldx #0 / loop: sta $0400,x / inx / cpx #40 / bne loop
unsigned char i; for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) { }
load "$",8 then list shows the directory
